content.intro: This lesson introduces git security fundamentals as part of Git Security and Professional Best Practices. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Git does not keep a file secret just because it is local, ignored or deleted in a later commit. Protect credentials, control remote access and understand where copies of a commit may already exist.

content_blocks.title: Git security boundaries
content_blocks.alt_text: Local history, remote permissions, credentials, signatures and hosted branch policies are separate controls. None can substitute for all the others.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Git does not keep a file secret just because it is local, ignored or deleted in a later commit. Protect credentials, control remote access and understand where copies of a commit may already exist.

For **Git Security Fundamentals**, keep the named subtopics in view: Repository access control; Local versus remote security; Protecting repository metadata; Understanding the limits of version control. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Local hooks can be bypassed and are not server-side enforcement. Never print or commit real credentials; use server/CI protections for shared policy.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

task: Create a checklist for the current repository covering ignored local files, credential handling, access permissions, and the verification evidence a teammate should review. Use fake example values only.

After the example, verify with git status --short --branch and/or git log --oneline --graph as appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
